source.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
source.authors: Yi-Ming Tang; Harshvardhan Saini; Zhao-Qian Yao; Zheng Lin; Yi-Zhen Liao; Jing-Yi Cui; Yi-Sen Wang; Mengnan Du; Dian-Bo Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. The displayed arXiv version metadata says v6, dated 2 May 2026, despite the supplied ID/year.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical results and experiments on sparse dictionary learning showing non-identifiability and polysemantic partial minima, refining how learned dictionary features should be interpreted. It does not directly test the toy-model geometry described in V1.
record.gate_note: The paper tests sparse dictionary learning (SDL), principally through theory, a synthetic feature-recovery benchmark, and CLIP representations. Table 1 and Table 2 report ground-truth recovery and maximum inner product; Table 1's results are included below. Table 2 uses class-mean embeddings as proxies, not known ground-truth features. Appendix G reports additional feature-recovery ablations over feature count, interference, sparsity, and TopK k; these are not separately extracted here. The Llama 3.1 resampling comparison reports training loss, not feature recovery or polysemanticity, so it is not a row for these versions. Theoretical statements and qualitative examples are recorded where they directly bear on the versions tested.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether sparse dictionaries recover the true features. It proves non-identifiability and spurious polysemantic partial minima, and measures ground-truth recovery for seven SDL methods on a synthetic benchmark with known features and on CLIP. This bears on V5 (SAE features as canonical units). Polysemanticity here is in the dictionary's latents, not the network's neurons, so V2 and V3 are not tested. V1 is not tested either: superposed features are built into the benchmark, not learned. Not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SDL is piecewise biconvex and non-identifiable. It admits zero-loss solutions that recover no ground-truth features, plus pervasive polysemantic partial minima that explain dead neurons and feature absorption. They propose feature anchoring to improve recovery, and argue that neuron resampling escapes partial minima, shown by lower loss on a Llama 3.1 SAE.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theoretical analysis and SDL feature-recovery study, not a reproduction of Toy Models of Superposition. It studies sparse dictionary learning, partial minima, and feature anchoring rather than toy-network feature geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported feature recovery varies with SDL method and anchoring; Appendix G additionally reports variation with feature count, interference, feature sparsity, and TopK k. Qualitative CLIP feature descriptions differ with anchoring.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 3.6: for any realizable polysemantic partition there is a positive-loss partial minimum of the SDL objective, even when latent dimension is at least the feature count. This is polysemanticity in dictionary latents without capacity shortage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemantic SAE latents can arise from optimization partial minima rather than insufficient dictionary capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 3.8: hierarchical concept structure makes feature-absorption activation patterns realizable, linking absorption to partial minima.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature absorption in SAEs follows from hierarchical feature structure.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says scripts will be provided upon acceptance but gives no URL.
record.problems: The central theory relies on representation assumptions, and the paper notes that extreme-sparsity results may not extend to moderate sparsity, real features may be correlated or non-one-dimensional, and convergence to global minima is not guaranteed. CLIP ground-truth feature directions are unavailable and class means are only proxies. The reported tables give no uncertainty estimates; qualitative examples are not systematic feature-level measurements.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix G Tables 4–7 report additional feature-recovery results over feature count/superposition ratio, maximum interference, sparsity, and TopK k; these are omitted rather than expanding the table with many method-by-setting comparisons. Figure 7's Llama 3.1 8B Instruct resampling result reports loss, not feature recovery or polysemanticity, so it does not bear directly on the tested versions.

untested.parts: Superposed features with interference M are built into the benchmark. No toy network is trained and its learned geometry or sparsity transition measured.
Capacity or importance allocation in model neurons is not studied. Polysemanticity is analysed only in SDL latents.
Polysemantic neurons of the original network are not studied.
No LLM feature recovery. The Llama 3.1 SAE reports training loss only, and CLIP is a vision model with proxy targets.
Stability across seeds and runs, and completeness of dictionaries for real model representations, are not tested.
1-D features are assumed. Non-1-D features are noted only as a limitation.

missing.what: Unanchored ReLU SAE GT recovery is 0% at every superposition ratio (n=800–1400, ratio 1.04x–1.82x), with MIP falling from 0.361 to 0.181.

Recovery by sparsity level. Unanchored TopK-family recovery is 95.6–99.7% at the 'S=0.1' setting versus 79–82% at 'S=0.005'. JumpReLU recovers 11.8% at S=0.005. The S labels conflict with Table 1's S=0.99, and the S=0.01 rows duplicate Table 1.
TopK k ablation: unanchored GT recovery is 100% at k=32, 93.9% at k=64 and 86.7% at k=128.
Recovery across maximum interference M=0.05, 0.2, 0.5. Unanchored TopK family stays about 84–86% and ReLU/JumpReLU stay at 0%.

record.verdict_notes: The anchored values in R3–R12 measure the authors' own method, not ordinary SAE behaviour. In R10–R12 anchoring trains toward the very class-mean directions used for evaluation, so anchored recovery there is near-circular. Sparsity labels in Tables 5 and 6 are inconsistent with Table 1: the Table 6 S=0.01 rows and the Table 5 M=0.05 rows reproduce Table 1 numbers. No uncertainty estimates or seeds are given, and code is not released. Some of the Linear Representation Bench (benchmark) results carry positive interference by construction, so it is a toy setting for V5 rather than a real model.

versions.untested_parts: The paper assumes sparse, linearly decomposed features and constructs synthetic representations with controlled interference, but does not measure whether learned directions form the claim's nearly orthogonal overlapping geometry or a sparsity-dependent geometric transition.

The paper analyzes polysemantic SDL latent units and shows partial minima can occur when nq≥n. It does not test an importance-based allocation rule, measure which features receive dedicated dimensions, or establish that this is the cause of polysemanticity in model neurons.

The alternative mechanism is established for SDL optimization and illustrated in learned dictionary features; the paper does not test polysemantic neurons in the original neural network independently of the dictionary learner.
The paper does not measure real language-model features distributed across neurons or assess whether an SAE recovers sparse features from an LLM. The Llama experiment reports loss only.
The paper tests feature recovery and demonstrates non-identifiability, but does not test the temporal stability of SAE features or whether a dictionary is complete for a model's representation.
The framework assumes one-dimensional feature directions and mentions non-one-dimensional features as a limitation; it does not compare one-dimensional and multidimensional features.

rows.subject: SDL (theoretical construction)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 3.6 constructs a partial minimum for any realizable, polysemantic activation pattern that partitions the features.
rows.measure: Existence of a polysemantic partial minimum with positive approximate loss
rows.value: For every such pattern, a partial minimum with positive loss exists.
rows.note: The result supplies an SDL optimization mechanism for polysemantic latent units; it does not establish the prevalence of this mechanism in trained neural networks. Its existence even when nq≥n bears against a capacity-only explanation.
rows.check: Theorem 3.6 concerns SDL latent units, not model neurons, so it does not bear on V2/V3 (moved to fits_no_version). It does bear on V5: positive-loss polysemantic partial minima exist for any realizable partition, so a learned dictionary need not be canonical. This is an existence proof, not a rate.

rows.operation_detail: Illustrates learned encoder and decoder directions that reconstruct without matching ground-truth features.

conditions.value: zero reconstruction loss without recovering ground-truth features

rows.measure: Ground-truth feature correspondence and reconstruction loss
rows.value: Learned encoder directions fail to align with ground truth while reconstruction loss is approximately zero.
rows.note: The paper presents this as an example of non-identifiability; it does not report a frequency for such solutions.
rows.check: Illustrative construction (Fig. 4). Near-zero loss with no correspondence to ground truth, i.e. non-identifiability. The underlying result is Theorem 3.4. No frequency is reported.

relationships.condition: ReLU and JumpReLU SAEs on the Linear Representation Bench, plus the theoretical results
relationships.reason: Unanchored ReLU and JumpReLU recover 0% of known features (MIP about 0.2). Theory shows zero-loss non-recovering solutions and polysemantic partial minima (R1–R4). Per the text, Table 4 shows ReLU SAEs at 0% for every superposition ratio from 1.04x to 1.82x.
relationships.display_finding: Unanchored ReLU and JumpReLU SAEs recovered 0% of known features (MIP about 0.2), and ReLU SAEs stayed at 0% at every superposition ratio from 1.04x to 1.82x. Theory shows zero-loss solutions that do not recover the features and polysemantic partial minima.

reader_labels.reason: Theorem 3.6 gives positive-loss polysemantic partial minima even in this non-undercomplete setting, so limited latent capacity is not required for that SDL phenomenon (R1). The paper does not test importance-based allocation.
